The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) is retaining most of its gains this year despite significant economic volatility and political change. Excitement about artificial intelligence (AI) and confidence in the economy are strong growth drivers, and the market has been rallying after a post-election drop.

But not every stock is enjoying a strong run this year. And while stocks that drop can scare investors, that's where you can often find the best opportunities. Dutch Bros (NYSE:BROS), MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI), and On Holding (NYSE:ONON) are all plunging this year, but they have fantastic long-term potential.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's why these three stocks could be great additions to your portfolio.

Image source: Dutch Bros.

1. Dutch Bros: Down 43%

Dutch Bros is a small coffee shop chain with big ambitions. It has created a unique model with exclusive customer beverages and a store portfolio that's mostly drive-thrus, and it has attracted a large customer base that keeps coming back for more.

Part of the company's success comes from its menu, which leans toward the sweet and cold, setting it apart from the classic coffee shop. People also love its friendly customer service and focus on speed.

Management has been at the forefront of beverage innovation, including being the first major chain to offer boba when it became popular two years ago and launching its own line of Myst healthy energy drinks.

Revenue increased 30% year over year in the third quarter, and same-shop sales were up 4.4%. Net income increased from $27.3 million to $37.2 million.

Dutch Bros has 1,273 locations as of the end of the third quarter, and management says it has visibility to reach its goal of 2,029 stores by 2029. That's nearly double today's count, which could lead to doubling revenue over the next four or so years from new stores alone.

The market, however, was disappointed by the lowered full-year guidance. Management is navigating inflation and higher costs, which are impacting the business from top to bottom.

However, the long-term outlook is very strong, and Dutch Bros should reward shareholders who hold for the long term.

2. MercadoLibre: Down 25%

MercadoLibre operates the largest e-commerce business in Latin America as well as a thriving financial platform, including what it expects to become the largest digital bank in Mexico.

title: Investors: If a Market Correction Is Coming, This 1 Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
detail:
Investors: If a Market Correction Is Coming, This 1 Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
Brett Schafer, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 2:05 PM EST 4 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stock market has begun to tumble — especially the technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out. In fact, the Nasdaq-100 index has already entered a correction, down over 11% from its highs.

Could the S&P 500 index follow suit? Market corrections are normal, and investors should expect them to occur on a regular basis. However, in order to mitigate the pain of market drawdowns, investors who buy individual stocks should utilize this one strategy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That strategy is diversification.

Why diversification matters

Diversification is the practice of keeping your savings in different baskets so that if one idea falls apart, you are not going to lose everything.

Most portfolios should have a minimum of 20-30 stocks to benefit from diversification. The Motley Fool recommends 50. There is some nuance to this: An investor with just $1,000 in savings should not feel the need to put it into 50 stocks. Wait until you have more in the bank account to slowly build out this portfolio.

Someone with six figures or seven figures in savings could definitely spread their savings over 50 or so stocks in order to stay properly diversified. That way, if one of the stocks you own goes to zero, the rest can pick up the slack.

Fifty stocks for an individual investor is a good sweet spot. Much more, and the portfolio can feel too crowded and overwhelming to manage. Much less, and you are exposed to massive amounts of volatility, which you may or may not want to experience.

More than just buying 50 stocks

Of course, there is even more nuance to building a portfolio than there is in having 50 stocks. One needs to consider what sectors to spread their bets around. If 40 of the 50 stocks you own are centered in a risky sector like AI, you may have significantly less diversification than you think.

Or, there is the risk of having one or two positions be massive in your portfolio. If the majority of your portfolio was Nvidia and Micron Technology this year, it wouldn't matter how many other stocks you own; they would be too insignificant to replace the massive drawdowns from these two AI infrastructure stocks.

Investors can also consider diversifying into different stock sizes, factors, and geographies, which tend to have uncorrelated performance. Factors can be complicated, but the most popular are value stocks, which are the statistically cheapest stocks on the market. Match them with some AI technology stocks, and your portfolio is starting to diversify quite quickly.

Kamina Bashir

^GSPC
USB
MSGE
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Photo by BeInCrypto

Wall Street's latest selloff has investors looking for somewhere safer to put their money. Bank of America sees potential in five stocks.

Yet three have fallen this year, while the broader US market has gained more than 10%.

The search for safer investments gained urgency on November 5, when an AI-led market crash erased roughly $2 trillion from US stocks in the first hour.

Investors feared the newly Democratic-controlled Congress could slow AI data center development.

Bank of America's picks offer alternatives to the AI trade. So far, only two have outperformed the S&P 500.

Bank of America Stock Picks' 2026 Performance Against the S&P 500. Source: Google Finance
Two Stocks Remain Largely Bullish

Madison Square Garden Entertainment (MSGE) is the standout. Shares have jumped nearly 48% this year, helped by major concerts, including Harry Styles performances. Bank of America expects its Christmas Spectacular to provide another boost, with more shows and stronger advance ticket sales.

U.S. Bancorp (USB) has risen nearly 18%. The bank sees room for earnings growth as older assets are repriced and fee income expands. Its turnaround still depends on the wider economy holding up.

The other three picks face a tougher test.

Three Stocks are Still Waiting For a Recovery

AT&T (T) is down more than 6%, despite remaining Bank of America's top US telecom pick. Analysts point to improving cash flow, its dividend and a $34 price target. The shares have yet to reflect that optimism.

L3Harris (LHX) has fallen about 7%. Bank of America likes the new CEO's focus on better execution and overseas sales. However, the company faces fresh scrutiny over its possible role in Friday's nationwide US flight stoppage.

Krispy Kreme (DNUT) has lost roughly 2.5%, despite a recent rebound. Analyst Sara Senatore said maintaining earnings guidance despite rising costs was:

"The clearest evidence yet that the turnaround savings are durable."

The five stocks show the challenge of finding safety during market turmoil. Madison Square Garden has already delivered a substantial rally. The three laggards still need to prove their recovery plans can translate into stronger share prices.

For investors, a Buy rating offers no guarantee against another selloff.

title: This Dividend King Yields 5 Times the S&P 500. Is It a Buy Now?

This Dividend King Yields 5 Times the S&P 500. Is It a Buy Now?
Dave Kovaleski, The Motley Fool

HRL
^GSPC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

The numbers around Hormel Foods' (NYSE:HRL) dividend are pretty impressive. On Nov. 16, it will have paid a dividend for 393 straight quarters, which translates to 98 years.

Yes, the maker of Spam, Hormel Chili, Black Label Bacon, Planters, and Skippy peanut butter, among others, has paid a dividend every quarter since it became a public company in 1928.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The company has increased its annual payout for the last 60 straight years, making it a Dividend King (a company that has raised its annual dividend for at least 50 consecutive years). Hormel Foods has a record of consistency that is very hard to match.

It also pays one of the highest yields among stocks that aren't real estate investment trusts (REITs) or business development companies (BDCs). Hormel pays a dividend yield of 5.27%, which is almost 5 times the average yield on the S&P 500.

This high-yield dividend stock has been a staple in investors' portfolios for decades, but is it still a buy?

Image source: Getty Images.

Dividend King

Through the first nine months of 2026, Hormel sales have ticked up to $8.96 billion from $8.92 billion the previous year. Adjusted earnings, excluding divestitures, impairments, and other one-time expenses, were up about 6% through the first nine months.

In the third quarter, net sales were off 2% to $2.96 billion while adjusted earnings rose 6% to $0.37 per share.

Operating cash flow skyrocketed 54% to $241 million, due to improved inventory management and better working capital performance.

For fiscal 2026, Hormel lowered its sales guidance to 1% to 2% growth, down from 1% to 4% previously. Adjusted earnings guidance, however, rose to $1.45 per share to $1.51 per share from the previous guidance of $1.43 per share to $1.51 per share.

60 years and counting

Hormel had some $840 million in cash and cash equivalents at the end of the third quarter, boosted by the sale of its operations in Brazil under the Ceratti brand.

But in September, Hormel announced that it was acquiring Brakebush Brothers, a chicken company, for $1.1 billion. The deal will close in the first quarter of 2027. It's part of Hormel's strategic repositioning to shed underperforming assets and increase its footprint in growth areas, like chicken. The price is pretty hefty and will draw down its cash position and raise its debt.

title: Why Cashing Out Your 401(k) at 55 Costs You $170K in Lost Growth
detail:
Why Cashing Out Your 401(k) at 55 Costs You $170K in Lost Growth
John Csiszar
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM EST 3 min read
^GSPC
sturti · Getty Images

If you leave your job, you can access your 401(k) money without the 10% early withdrawal penalty as early as age 55. But that doesn't necessarily mean age 55 is a "green light."

If you look at the money that you're leaving on the table by withdrawing it that early, it can be eye-opening.

Consider This: FREE 2026 Investor Guide + Up to $25,000 in Silver with Qualifying Purchases

How Much a $100K Cash-Out Can Actually Cost

According to Vanguard, the S&P 500, along with its predecessor index the S&P Composite, produced an average annual return of about 10.5% since 1926.

Now, imagine a worker who leaves a job at 55 and cashes out a $100,000 401(k) fund. If that worker had instead left that money invested in the S&P 500 for another 10 years, to the common retirement age of 65. Using the historical average, that $100,000 could have grown to about $271,400 instead. That worker would be leaving over $171,000 on the table in just a single decade.

The real variable in the scenario is what a worker does with the money upon withdrawal. If used for living expenses and general spending, that worker could end up with $0 at age 65, instead of over $271,000 if the money was left in the 401(k) account. Plus, at age 65, that money would have to fund a shorter retirement. A withdrawal at age 55 means that money has to help cover an additional decade of life after work.

10 Years Is the Short Version

Although 65 has often been cited as a common retirement target, for most workers, the Social Security Administration considers 67 to be "full retirement age." Some workers don't tap their benefits until age 70.

If you extend the same $100,000 out to 15 years instead of 10, that balance would grow to roughly $447,200 instead of $271,000. That's more than four times the original balance. As a side benefit, waiting to retire until age 70 would also maximize the amount of Social Security benefits the worker would receive. Payouts increase by 8% each year from age 67 to age 70, boosting monthly checks by 24% for those with the patience to wait, per the SSA.

You Still Owe Taxes

Although you can sidestep the 10% early withdrawal rule by separating from an employer at age 55, you still can't avoid the IRS. The money you withdraw from your 401(k) plan is fully taxable as ordinary income, whether you take it out at age 35, 55 or 75.

Depending on your outside income, this could amount to a huge tax bill. If you work a full year, retire in December and withdraw from your 401(k) acount that same year, for example, you'd be adding a retirement distribution on top of your full year's income. That may be enough to push you into a higher tax bracket.

3 Beaten-Down Stocks Under $10 to Buy in November

NVDA
^GSPC
MU
AMD

It's almost the middle of November. And boy, oh boy -- what a month it's been.

However you slice it, the market has been tinged with volatility. Just look at the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC): The index suffered a huge sell-off in the post-election days of uncertainty, only to stage a quick and powerful recovery a few days later. Meanwhile, AI's biggest winners -- Nvidia, Micron Technology, and Advanced Micro Devices, to name a few -- have also taken a beating, with investors growing worried about inflation and valuations at the same time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Sharp declines, in general, can create buying opportunities for patient and perspicacious investors, but not every beaten-down stock will be a genuine bargain. In particular, I'm looking at growth stocks in emerging industries, many of which have sustained heavy damage in 2026. If you're willing to stomach the volatility, the following three growth stocks might be worth a closer look.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Archer Aviation

Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) is one of the frontrunners in the emerging electric air taxi market. Its Midnight aircraft, which can take off and land vertically like a helicopter, could offer travelers a way to soar over congested roads in cities around the world.

Earlier in 2026, Archer entered the fourth and final stage of the FAA type certification, the completion of which would bring it one step closer to launching commercial passenger services. The company eked out about $5 million in third-quarter revenue, while also sustaining a hefty $275 million loss that same quarter. These losses are heavy, but it is arguably the price Archer must pay to launch its novel eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) technology.

Despite its losses, Archer has been making good progress. Recently, it received FAA authorization to begin piloted demonstrations of Midnight in Los Angeles, where it will serve as the official air taxi provider for the 2028 Olympics. It's also in the midst of acquiring three subsidiaries from Boeing, one of which generates more than $200 million in annual revenue.

2. Joby Aviation

Like Archer, Joby Aviation (NYSE:JOBY) is developing electric air taxis for urban transportation. It is, however, farther along than Archer in the FAA's certification process, having already begun testing in the fifth and final stage of its certification process (Joby reports its progress in five stages, while Archer uses four phases).
